RemoteEvolver: Expanding Earth Observation Capabilities
through Agent Harness Evolution

Shengxiang Xu    Liang Yao    Shuyi Chen Affiliation:  Southeast University  Hohai University    Yishu Wang    Shimin Di    Fan Liu    Bishun Yao Affiliation:  Southeast University  Hohai University    Hanghui Guo    Xinyu Liu Affiliation:  The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Chengye Liang    Yuyu Luo Affiliation:  The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Min-Ling Zhang
Abstract

We are interested in developing a continually self-improving remote sensing agentic system. It should identify and address its capability gaps, retaining the resulting improvements to enhance performance on subsequent tasks. However, existing systems typically rely on fixed toolsets and confine their experience accumulation to re-orchestrating predefined capabilities, constraining both capability expansion and the transfer of improvements across tasks. As the infrastructure for agentic systems, the harness manages tools and workflow knowledge as editable, persistent resources outside the base model. These resources can therefore be updated and reused across tasks without additional post-training. Based on these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, an external harness for remote sensing agents that drives tool and workflow evolution through execution feedback. With the base model parameters fixed, RemoteEvolver acquires missing specialized tools on demand and distills verified successful execution experience from individual tasks into agent skills that can be reused across tasks. The acquired tools and accumulated skills jointly support planning and execution on subsequent tasks. Experiments on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench show that RemoteEvolver achieves average accuracy gains of 8.18 and 23.86 percentage points over its initial state when tools are fully available and partially missing. Under the same settings, it also outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by an average of 6.77 and 17.10 percentage points, respectively.

1 Introduction

Remote sensing agents autonomously plan and invoke perception models and geospatial analysis tools to perform Earth observation tasks [29, 9, 23, 21, 22] according to users’ queries. However, user requests sometimes exceed a system’s current capabilities in practical deployment. As illustrated in Fig. 1, an agent may understand a request [33, 10, 28, 15] and formulate a reasonable plan [2, 31, 25, 17], yet still fail to complete the task because a required specialized tool is unavailable. To support users’ analytical queries over time, remote sensing agents must develop self-evolving capabilities, autonomously identifying and addressing capability gaps during execution, and retaining verified improvements for reuse in subsequent tasks.

To achieve self-evolution, recent remote sensing agentic systems have explored various strategies, ranging from workflow repair and experience accumulation [24, 2, 25, 4] to on-demand script generation by proactively consulting documentation [35]. Despite this progress, these approaches primarily focus on optimizing their internal logic or generating simple rule-based scripts. Such script-level adaptations remain fundamentally constrained when task requirements exceed the perception capabilities supported by the agent’s existing toolset. Workflow adjustment and code generation alone cannot provide specialized capabilities that require pretrained models. To bridge these gaps, agents need to autonomously discover, acquire, and integrate pretrained models from external resources.

To effectively integrate these newly acquired models and corresponding practical experiences, agents can leverage their harness [7], which is the runtime support layer connecting the base model to the execution environment. As the infrastructure for agentic systems in Fig. 1, the harness manages tools and workflow knowledge as editable, persistent resources outside the base model. Consequently, modifying harness allows the system to seamlessly archive and reuse acquired capabilities across tasks. This external integration inherently bypasses the continuous training overhead required by approaches that attempt to internalize new capabilities through model parameter optimization [32, 26].

Motivated by these observations, we propose RemoteEvolver, a self-evolving harness for remote sensing agents that connects capability acquisition with the accumulation of reusable experience. With the base model parameters frozen, it supports continued capability growth through two complementary mechanisms: dynamic toolset expansion and skill library consolidation. Dynamic toolset expansion enables agents to autonomously acquire and integrate pretrained models from open-source repositories as task requirements evolve. Skill library consolidation distills verified successful executions into reusable procedures that guide subsequent tasks. Crucially, successful workflows involving newly acquired tools can also be consolidated into reusable skills, allowing new capabilities to be retained together with the procedural knowledge needed to apply them. It enables remote sensing agents to build on both advances in the external model ecosystem and their own accumulated execution experience across tasks.

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of RemoteEvolver on Earth-Bench [5] and OpenEarthAgent-Bench [18] with fixed base model parameters. By actively evolving its external harness, the system achieves average accuracy improvements of 23.86%\% and 8.18%\% over its initial state when tools are partially missing and fully available, respectively. Besides, under the same settings, RemoteEvolver significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods by an average of 17.10%\% and 6.77%\%. Furthermore, extensive analysis confirms that this evolution paradigm generalizes well across various mainstream foundation models, consistently delivering strong transferability on diverse remote sensing tasks.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a harness-centric self-evolution paradigm for Earth observation agents, enabling continual capability growth without updating the base model parameters.

  • •

    We propose RemoteEvolver, a practical framework that enables the agentic system to incorporate emerging specialized models into agent systems and build upon accumulated task experience across tasks.

  • •

    Extensive evaluations demonstrate that RemoteEvolver significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods under both complete and constrained tool settings.

2 Related Work

2.1 Model-Centric Earth Observation Systems

Advances in pretraining have broadened the capabilities of model-centric Earth observation systems in representation learning, semantic understanding, and spatial prediction. For instance, SatMAE [3] learns transferable representations from temporal or multispectral satellite imagery. Broader input coverage is achieved through optical–SAR imagery fusion in CROMA [6] and SkySense [8], with AnySat [1] further unifying data across resolutions, scales and modalities. Language-based capabilities have expanded from image–text alignment, as illustrated by RemoteCLIP [13], to richer forms of interaction. These include image-level and region-level dialogue in GeoChat [11] and interactive understanding of multi-sensor and multi-temporal observations in EarthDial [20]. Spatial prediction has also seen parallel advances toward more flexible outputs. RemoteSAM [30] unifies multiple perception tasks around referring expression segmentation, whereas GeoGround [36] represents horizontal and oriented bounding boxes and segmentation masks in a common format. GeoPixel [19] further connects conversational understanding with pixel-level segmentation. By structuring these versatile capabilities into an autonomous reasoning workflow, RemoteReasoner [31] bridges the gap between foundational perception and end-to-end task execution. Together, these developments provide a growing range of remote sensing capabilities. With appropriate task adaptation, the resulting models can be exposed through callable interfaces as specialized tools for agents tackling complex tasks.

2.2 Agentic Earth Observation Systems

Agentic Earth observation systems coordinate domain-specific models and processing tools to translate user requests into executable workflows. RS-Agent [29] and Earth-Agent [5] combine specialized tools with domain knowledge to solve remote sensing tasks, while RemoteAgent [33] routes requests between internal models and external experts according to task requirements. To support workflow construction and adaptation, OpenEarth-Agent [35] generates task-specific tool scripts and iteratively repairs workflows. Earth-Agent-Pro [14] uses domain skills and execution evidence to repair affected downstream steps, while RSMeM [24] reflects on failures to improve subsequent attempts on the same task. Further work explores experience-driven approaches to improving planning and execution reliability. CangLing-KnowFlow [2] consolidates successfully adapted workflows into reusable templates and derives repair rules from failures. GeoEvolver [4] accumulates tool-use experience from successful and failed exploration trajectories. GeoForge [25] organizes execution knowledge at multiple levels through workflow graphs, action-level experience, and standard operating procedures for skills. Despite these advances, a critical limitation persists: these systems primarily rely on pre-integrated tools, limiting their ability to autonomously handle tasks that require integrating additional specialized external tools.

3 RemoteEvolver

We propose RemoteEvolver in Fig. 2, which integrates both tool evolution and workflow evolution as two complementary components. Specifically, these two core components are realized through dynamic toolset expansion and skill library consolidation, respectively. By continually updating the external harness while keeping the base model parameters fixed, it enables agents to accumulate and reuse new capabilities across diverse remote sensing tasks.

3.1 Problem Formulation

We consider a sequence of remote sensing tasks {zt=(qt,xt)}t=1N\{z_{t}=(q_{t},x_{t})\}_{t=1}^{N}, where qtq_{t} denotes a natural-language instruction and xtx_{t} denotes the associated input data. Let MθM_{\theta} be the base model, whose parameters θ\theta remain fixed throughout evolution. To achieve capability accumulation independent of model parameters, we represent the evolving persistent state of the external harness as

Ht=(𝒯t,𝒮t),H_{t}=(\mathcal{T}_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t}), (1)

where 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} is the available toolset providing executable operations, and 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} is a library of skill documents acting as the system’s long-term memory to provide procedural knowledge. Together, they support the dynamic generation of task-specific reasoning workflows.

Given task ztz_{t}, the agent plans an initial workflow Wt(0)W_{t}^{(0)} and execute step-by-step based on the current harness HtH_{t}. Crucially, if a capability bottleneck or unsatisfactory intermediate outcome is encountered during execution, the agent can on-demand acquire missing tools, updating the harness to an intermediate state H~t\widetilde{H}_{t} and dynamically adapting the workflow to resume the task. If no tool acquisition is triggered, the harness remains unchanged (H~t=Ht\widetilde{H}_{t}=H_{t}). This interleaved planning and execution process is formulated as:

Wt(0)\displaystyle W_{t}^{(0)} =Planθ⁡(zt;Ht),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Plan}_{\theta}(z_{t};H_{t}), (2)
(y^t,τt,Wt,H~t)\displaystyle(\hat{y}_{t},\tau_{t},W_{t},\widetilde{H}_{t}) =Executeθ⁡(zt,Wt(0),Ht),\displaystyle=\operatorname{Execute}_{\theta}(z_{t},W_{t}^{(0)};H_{t}),

where Wt(0)W_{t}^{(0)} is the initial workflow generated by the base model, WtW_{t} is the final executed workflow, y^t\hat{y}_{t} is the task output, and τt\tau_{t} is the detailed execution trace. Given verification feedback ftf_{t} provided by a external evaluator, the harness is subsequently updated as

Ht+1=Update⁡(H~t,Wt,zt,τt,ft).H_{t+1}=\operatorname{Update}(\widetilde{H}_{t},W_{t},z_{t},\tau_{t},f_{t}). (3)

This evolutionary process is driven by a complementary mechanism: registering verified new tools into the toolset and distilling successful workflow WtW_{t} into reusable skills.

Our objective is to push capability boundaries and improve performance on subsequent tasks through continuous updates to the external harness, without modifying parameters θ\theta. During evaluation, the harness state HtH_{t} is strictly frozen, and test feedback is excluded from evolution.

3.2 Dynamic Toolset Expansion

When the current toolset 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} lacks a required remote sensing operation or fails to yield satisfactory execution outcomes, RemoteEvolver searches GitHub and HuggingFace for relevant implementations and pretrained models. This search process is driven by the capability gap between the current task ztz_{t} and the available toolset 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t}. To select resources for deployment, the system matches the functional requirements and IO constraints against candidate resources, such as README files or model documentation. This selection process specifically evaluates supported operations, applicable data modalities, and output formats. Let the initially retrieved candidate tool set be:

𝒰t=Search⁡(zt,𝒯t).\mathcal{U}_{t}=\operatorname{Search}(z_{t},\mathcal{T}_{t}). (4)

For each selected resource, the system retrieves code, prepares the runtime environment, and constructs a callable interface. For tools based on pretrained models, it also automatically downloads and deploys the required weights. We represent each deployed candidate tool u∈𝒰tu\in\mathcal{U}_{t} as:

u=(r,ω,ℰ,g),u=(r,\omega,\mathcal{E},g), (5)

where rr denotes the retrieved implementation, ω\omega represents the pretrained weights, ℰ\mathcal{E} signifies the runtime environment, and gg stands for the interface. The interface is responsible for receiving task data and operational parameters, invoking the underlying implementation, and returning results. For tools that do not rely on pretrained models, we set ω=∅\omega=\varnothing.

Each candidate tool u∈𝒰tu\in\mathcal{U}_{t} undergoes an execution check. If an invocation fails, the system uses the returned error information to revise the interface adapter code and repeats the check. Let 𝒱exec​(u)∈{0,1}\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{exec}}(u)\in\{0,1\} denote the final execution check outcome. The set of accepted tools is:

𝒰tpass={u∈𝒰t∣𝒱exec​(u)=1}.\mathcal{U}_{t}^{\mathrm{pass}}=\left\{u\in\mathcal{U}_{t}\mid\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{exec}}(u)=1\right\}. (6)

Tools that pass the execution check are registered in the toolset, yielding the updated available toolset:

𝒯~t=𝒯t∪𝒰tpass.\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}_{t}=\mathcal{T}_{t}\cup\mathcal{U}_{t}^{\mathrm{pass}}. (7)

The newly registered specialized tools are immediately available to support the current task’s execution, enabling the dynamic adaptation of the workflow, and persistently retained for reuse in subsequent tasks.

3.3 Skill Library Consolidation

Tool acquisition expands the underlying operations available to the system. To reuse execution experience, RemoteEvolver distills verified workflows into skill.md documents and preserves them in a persistent skill library. These documents explicitly guide and condition subsequent workflow planning by providing detailed structured step constraints and tool dependencies.

Given a task ztz_{t}, the system retrieves a set of relevant skills 𝒦t\mathcal{K}_{t} from the current skill library 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t}:

𝒦t=Retrieveθ⁡(zt,𝒮t).\mathcal{K}_{t}=\operatorname{Retrieve}_{\theta}(z_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t}). (8)

The planner would read these documents and combines their structured guidance with the current remote sensing data and task requirements to construct and dynamically adapt the initial execution workflow:

Wt(0)=Planθ⁡(zt,𝒯t,𝒦t),W_{t}^{(0)}=\operatorname{Plan}_{\theta}(z_{t};\mathcal{T}_{t},\mathcal{K}_{t}), (9)

where 𝒯t\mathcal{T}_{t} denotes the toolset currently available during the initial planning phase. The retrieved skills guide the selection of processing steps and parameters. If no applicable skill is found, we set 𝒦t=∅\mathcal{K}_{t}=\varnothing, and the planner directly generates a workflow from the task requirements and the existing toolset. If tool evolution is triggered during execution, the system leverages the newly acquired tools to dynamically adapt and finalize the workflow into WtW_{t}.

After task completion, the system performs a closed-loop update of the skill library using the final workflow WtW_{t}, execution trace τt\tau_{t}, and task feedback ftf_{t}. Verified successful workflows are distilled into new skills by the base model θ\theta. Concurrently, existing skills are revised, merged, or deactivated based on their historical reuse outcomes, which are tracked as success rates and invocation counts. Deactivated skills will no longer participate in subsequent planning stages. This update process can be expressed as:

𝒮t+1=Updateθ⁡(𝒮t,Wt,zt,τt,ft).\mathcal{S}_{t+1}=\operatorname{Update}_{\theta}(\mathcal{S}_{t},W_{t},z_{t},\tau_{t},f_{t}). (10)

If newly acquired tools are invoked in a successful workflow, their complete usage procedures are also retained within the generated skill documents, thereby directly supporting future workflow planning through retrieval.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets. We evaluate RemoteEvolver on Earth-Bench [5] and OpenEarthAgent-Bench [18]. We split tasks into evolution and test sets at a ratio of 7:3. When splitting, we aim to keep task category distribution similar in both sets.

Baselines. We compare RemoteEvolver with 5 representative remote sensing agent systems, including RSMeM [24], RS-Agent [29], Earth-Agent [5], OpenEarthAgent [18], and RemoteAgent [33]. We additionally include our initial system RemoteEvolver∗ as an internal baseline.

Implementation Details. In the main experiments, we use Qwen3.8 27B [16] as the backbone for all methods except OpenEarthAgent and RemoteAgent, which retain their officially released checkpoints. We further evaluate RemoteEvolver with GPT-5.6 Luna, Qwen3.8 Max [16], DeepSeek V4.1 Flash [27], MiniMax M3 [12], and GLM 5.3 [34]. Within each method, the same model serves as both the planner and executor. All models operate in thinking mode with the temperature set to 0. We impose no explicit limits on execution steps or output tokens. The tool execution environment is equipped with 8 NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. More implementation details are provided in Appendix.

4.2 Evaluation Protocol

Tool Availability. We consider two tool settings. Tool-Available initially provides a complete toolset covering all tasks, whereas Tool-Missing initially provides a predefined subset of the full toolset, consisting of basic remote sensing tools. Detailed tool lists are provided in Appendix.

Evaluation Procedure. We divide evolution process into 8 stages and save the harness state HtH_{t} after each stage, where t=0,1,…,8t=0,1,\dots,8. We evaluate all harness states on the same testset. The harness state remains frozen during evaluation, and test feedback is not used for subsequent evolution.

Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate system evolutionary process in terms of task performance, transferability and retention capability. We measure task performance with accuracy Acc⁡(H,D)=1|D|​∑q∈Daq\mathrm{Acc}(H,D)=\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_{q\in D}a_{q}, where HH denotes the harness state, DD denotes the testset, and aq∈{0,1}a_{q}\in\{0,1\} represents the binary correctness of task q∈Dq\in D.

To measure the system’s transferability, we further split the testset DD into the near subset DNearD_{\mathrm{Near}} and the far subset DFarD_{\mathrm{Far}}. The near subset DNearD_{\mathrm{Near}} contains tasks similar to those in evolution, while the far subset DFarD_{\mathrm{Far}} contains tasks unseen during evolutionary process. Then, we utilize forward transfer (FWT) to measure the transferability gain of the current state HtH_{t} over the initial state H0H_{0}:

FWTg(t)=Acc⁡(Ht,Dg)−Acc⁡(H0,Dg),\mathrm{FWT_{g}^{(t)}}=\mathrm{Acc}(H_{t},D_{g})-\mathrm{Acc}(H_{0},D_{g}), (11)

where g∈{Near,Far}g\in\{\mathrm{Near},\mathrm{Far}\} and DgD_{g} denotes the corresponding test subset. Higher FWT indicates better transferability.

We also measure retention capability as the proportion of previously solved tasks that current system fails to solve. For each task q∈Dq\in D, let aq(t−1)a_{q}^{(t-1)} and aq(t)a_{q}^{(t)} denote its binary correctness on the last attempt and under the current harness state HtH_{t}, respectively. We define Retention Rate (RR) as:

RRt=∑q∈D𝕀⁡(aq(t−1)=1∧aq(t)=0)∑q∈D𝕀⁡(aq(t−1)=1),\mathrm{RR}_{t}=\frac{\sum_{q\in D}\mathbb{I}(a_{q}^{(t-1)}=1\land a_{q}^{(t)}=0)}{\sum_{q\in D}\mathbb{I}(a_{q}^{(t-1)}=1)}, (12)

where 𝕀⁡(⋅)\mathbb{I}(\cdot) denotes the indicator function. A lower RR indicates better retention capability.

4.3 Main Results

Initial tool limitations expose a critical vulnerability in static remote sensing agentic systems. As shown in Table 1, transitioning from the Tool-Available to the Tool-Missing setting causes a catastrophic performance drop across all evaluated baselines, with an average accuracy degradation of 14.32 percentage points. For instance, Earth-Agent’s accuracy on Earth-Bench drops from 48.57%\% to 21.43%\%, highlighting its rigid dependence on pre-integrated toolsets.

RemoteEvolver fundamentally overcomes this bottleneck through dynamic harness evolution. Under the constrained Tool-Missing setting, our system autonomously expands its toolset and distills execution experience, achieving an average accuracy gain of 23.86 percentage points over its initial state. Remarkably, RemoteEvolver operating with initially missing tools (e.g., achieving 47.14%\% on Earth-Bench) can approach or even surpass the performance of the strongest external baselines equipped with the complete toolsets. This demonstrates the system’s strong resilience when facing severe capability gaps.

Furthermore, the benefits of harness evolution extend beyond merely bridging gaps. It also continuously pushes the performance upper bound. Even under the Tool-Available setting where no new tools are required, RemoteEvolver continues to optimize its procedural workflows, yielding an additional average gain of 8.18 percentage points. On Earth-Bench, while our initial system already establishes a strong baseline at 50.00%\%, the evolutionary process further elevates the state-of-the-art accuracy to 55.71%\%.

4.4 Ablation Study

We conduct comprehensive ablation studies to disentangle the individual contributions of tool and skill evolution. As shown in Table 2, while both mechanisms independently improve system performance, their effectiveness and degree of contribution depend heavily on initial tool constraints.

Under the Tool-Missing setting, bridging underlying capability gaps serves as the primary prerequisite for evolution. Enabling only skill evolution yields limited gains, improving accuracy by merely 5.72 and 9.58 percentage points on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench, respectively. It indicates that accumulated procedural experience alone cannot compensate for the absence of core perception models. Conversely, enabling only tool evolution delivers substantial performance leaps, boosting accuracy by 27.14 and 14.90 percentage points across the two benchmarks.

Once tool constraints are lifted, the independent value of skill evolution becomes evident. Under the Tool-Available setting, where tool evolution is naturally disabled, continuously distilling skills still yields accuracy gains of 5.71 and 10.64 percentage points across 2 benchmarks. It demonstrates that equipping an agent with complete toolsets does not equate to optimal problem-solving capability. Instead, the system must continuously refine its tool orchestration and invocation logic through accumulated experience.

4.5 Evolution Trends

As shown in Fig. 3, while the overall accuracy initially rises, subsequent checkpoints reveal a non-monotonic trend. Specifically, while near-domain transfer FWTNear\mathrm{FWT}_{\mathrm{Near}} remains largely positive, far-domain transfer FWTFar\mathrm{FWT}_{\mathrm{Far}} suffers from severe fluctuations, sometimes dropping below 0 on OpenEarthAgent-Bench. Simultaneously, the retention rate abnormally increases, indicating the agent forgets previously mastered tasks. These observations highlight a critical insight: simply expanding the harness does not guarantee stable performance growth. Thus, we conduct a deep analysis and attribute this non-monotonic degradation to a cascading effect across three levels of the agent’s expanded action space: tool exploration, skill retrieval, and workflow execution, as illustrated in Appendix.

First, over-exploration at the tool level. While recovering missing tools equips the agent with essential capabilities, it introduces increased decision noise into planning. Consequently, the agent tends to over-complicate originally simple tasks by repeatedly invoking irrelevant newly-acquired tools, ultimately leading to failure via exhausted execution rounds or the gradual accumulation of intermediate errors.

Second, negative transfer at the skill level. Even when the correct tools are selected, distilled skills encapsulating general rules may possess vague applicability boundaries. This ambiguity causes the system to retrieve seemingly relevant historical skills that actually conflict with the constraints of the new task, thereby misguiding the workflow.

Finally, execution loss at the planning level. Even if an appropriate skill is retrieved, the agent may still fail to strictly follow its guidelines. During reasoning processes, the internal planner frequently overlooks critical constraints within the skill document, resulting in a disconnect between semantic comprehension and actual execution.

4.6 Further Analysis

To provide deeper insights into the mechanisms and practical advantages of RemoteEvolver, we further systematically explore the following core questions.

Does external harness evolution generalize universally across diverse foundation models? As illustrated in Fig. 4, we extend our framework to 6 diverse foundation models under the Tool-Missing setting. Regardless of their varying parameter sizes and initial capabilities, all evaluated models consistently expand their capabilities, achieving positive accuracy gains and improved near-domain transfer.

Notably, a model’s initial zero-shot performance does not strictly dictate its evolutionary potential. For instance, GPT-5.6 Luna does not possess the highest initial accuracy, trailing the 18.57%\% of GLM 5.3. However, it exhibits exceptional capability in assimilating external tools and experiences, securing a massive 42.86%\% boost to reach the highest absolute accuracy of 58.57%\%. These results confirm that external harness evolution is a universally applicable paradigm that thoroughly decouples continuous system growth from the inherent limits of static internal weights.

How do agents dynamically expand and recover toolsets under missing conditions? We further analyze the final toolset composition after evolution. As shown in Fig. 5, the agents exhibit robust dynamic expansion capabilities, transitioning from passive recovery to proactive exploration.

Tool recovery capacity is highly correlated with the model’s final task performance. On Earth-Bench, where all models are restricted to 63 initial tools, powerful foundation models, such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GPT-5.6 Luna, successfully recovered 13 and 12 core tools. Conversely, models like MiniMax M3 only managed to recover 1 tool, leaving 22 tools persistently missing, which directly explains its suboptimal accuracy observed in Q1.

The system also exhibits open-ended discovery beyond predefined boundaries. The agents did not confine their exploration to the predefined full set of tools. As illustrated in Fig. 5, multiple models successfully acquired extra tools absent from the original full set. Most notably, the top-performing GPT-5.6 Luna autonomously introduced 8 extra tools to address the unique demands of complex tasks. This phenomenon provides evidence that RemoteEvolver endows agents with open-ended toolset expansion capabilities, thoroughly liberating them from the constraints of static tool libraries to achieve true on-demand growth.

Is the computational overhead of harness evolution justified by Pareto efficiency? Continuously invoking external tools and retrieving historical skills inherently increases prompt lengths and execution rounds. To verify whether this computational overhead is acceptable, we map test accuracy against token consumption in Fig. 7. Although the full RemoteEvolver naturally consumes more tokens than static baselines like EarthAgent or RSMem, it establishes a distinctly dominant Pareto front across both benchmarks.

How are successful execution workflows distilled into structured reusable skills? Unlike traditional methods that attempt to internalize experience into model weights, RemoteEvolver distills verified successful execution trajectories into human-readable and structured skill documents. As illustrated in Fig. 6, a successfully verified spatial measurement workflow is preserved with explicitly defined scopes, input formats, and critical reuse constraints. This structural clarity guarantees reliable retrieval and precise execution in subsequent tasks.

How does RemoteEvolver overcome capability gaps and avoid error propagation in complex scenarios? As illustrated in Fig. 8, we demonstrate how RemoteEvolver tackles complex remote sensing tasks through concrete execution trajectories. In Fig. 8(a), when tasked with evaluating drought impacts, the initial agent relies solely on basic OpenCV thresholding and fails due to inaccurate lake boundary extraction. By enabling tool evolution, the agent autonomously acquires RemoteSAM to precisely map the water boundary and successfully completes the task.

In Fig. 8(b), when tracking urban building changes without historical experience, the agent directly computes mask differences, leading to massive false detections caused by sensor shifts. By applying historical skills, the agent learns to align images using invariant features before extracting masks, isolating structural changes and achieving accurate task completion. These cases demonstrate that tool expansion breaks through perceptual ceilings, while skill consolidation regularizes complex reasoning paths, jointly ensuring robust agent execution in complex environments.

5 Limitation

While RemoteEvolver demonstrates promising progress, there remain controllable limitations to address. As revealed in the evolution trend analysis in Section 4.6, unconstrained harness evolution can sometimes lead to non-monotonic performance fluctuations, such as degraded far-domain transfer and the forgetting of previously mastered tasks. This is primarily driven by a cascading effect caused by over-exploration at the tool level, negative transfer at the skill level, and execution loss at the planning level. Future work will focus on incorporating robust skill verification mechanisms and efficient evolution pruning strategies. These improvements aim to better control computational overhead and suppress decision noise while ensuring continuous capability growth, ultimately achieving more stable, reliable, and monotonic system evolution over time.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we explore the continuous self-improvement of remote sensing agentic systems when encountering capability gaps. To advance this direction, we propose RemoteEvolver, a novel harness-centric self-evolving paradigm. This framework provides the community with a practical training-free solution that enables agents to seamlessly integrate emerging external specialized models and reuse accumulated execution experience across tasks. Our evaluations show that RemoteEvolver establishes a new state-of-the-art on Earth-Bench and OpenEarthAgent-Bench under both complete and constrained tool settings. Ultimately, we hope this work catalyzes a paradigm shift in remote sensing agent community, moving beyond reliance on static, pre-integrated toolsets toward developing intelligent systems equipped with continuous self-growing capabilities.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
